title: Linear regression as projection
summary: Least squares picks the line whose squared residuals add up to the least. Seen as vectors, every possible prediction lies on a plane spanned by the feature columns, and the best prediction is the perpendicular shadow of the target vector on that plane, which gives the normal equations.
llm_link: Researchers test whether a language model's hidden vectors encode a property (a date, a location, whether a statement is true) by fitting a linear model on those vectors, a linear probe. If a projection predicts the property well, the information is laid out linearly inside the model.
key_ideas: A line predicts ŷ = w·x + b; a residual is actual minus predicted. Least squares minimises Σ residual².
Stack the targets into one vector y. Every prediction Xw is a combination of the columns of X (the feature column and a column of ones), so all predictions lie in the span of those columns.
The best prediction ŷ is the projection of y onto that span: the residual y − ŷ is perpendicular to every column.
Perpendicular means Xᵀ(y − Xw) = 0, which rearranges to the normal equations XᵀX w = Xᵀy.
In code, prefer np.linalg.lstsq (or solve) over inverting XᵀX; check that Xᵀr ≈ 0 and, with an intercept, Σr ≈ 0.

quiz.q: A house has actual price 50 and the line predicts 44. What is its residual?
quiz.explain: Residual = actual − predicted = 50 − 44 = 6. Least squares then squares it (36) before adding it to the total.

quiz.q: Predict the result: you fit least squares to the points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 5). What is the sum of squared residuals of the best line?
options: It depends on the starting guess
quiz.explain: The three points lie exactly on y = 2x + 1, so y is already inside the plane of possible predictions. Its projection is itself and every residual is 0. Least squares has no starting guess: the answer is unique.

quiz.q: In the vector picture, why is the residual vector perpendicular to the plane of predictions at the best fit?
options: Because squared numbers are always positive
Because the closest point on a plane to y is where the connecting arrow meets the plane at a right angle
Because the column of ones forces it
It is only perpendicular when the data has no noise
quiz.explain: Any other point on the plane is further from y (Pythagoras: the extra sideways distance adds to the squared length). Shortest residual = perpendicular residual = least squares.

quiz.q: Why does the design matrix X get a column of ones?
options: So the model can learn an intercept b: w·x + b·1
quiz.explain: Each prediction is w·(area) + b·1. Without the ones column the line is forced through the origin. A side effect: because the residual is perpendicular to the ones column, the residuals sum to zero.

quiz.q: A researcher fits a linear model from a language model's hidden vectors to the year each sentence mentions, and it predicts well on held-out sentences. What does this suggest?
options: The model memorised the test set
Information about the year is encoded roughly linearly in the hidden vectors
The model was trained with linear regression
Hidden vectors are lists of years
quiz.explain: This is a linear probe: a projection of the hidden vector recovers the year, so the information is laid out along a direction the probe can find. It says nothing about how the model itself was trained.

problems.title: The best line, from sums
problems.prompt:
For one feature, least squares has a closed form. With means x̄ and ȳ:

w = Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)  /  Σ (xᵢ − x̄)²
b = ȳ − w·x̄

Write fit_line(xs, ys) with plain Python lists that returns the tuple (w, b). Each Σ runs over the pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ) together, which is exactly what zip gives you.

If every x is the same, no line can be fitted (the denominator is 0): raise a ValueError.

fit_line([0, 1, 2], [1, 3, 5])   # (2.0, 1.0)

tests.name: exact line
tests.code:
w, b = fit_line([0, 1, 2], [1, 3, 5])
assert abs(w - 2) < 1e-9 and abs(b - 1) < 1e-9, f'points on y = 2x + 1 should give (2, 1), got ({w}, {b})'

tests.name: noisy data
tests.code:
w, b = fit_line([1, 2, 3, 4], [2, 3, 5, 6])
assert abs(w - 1.4) < 1e-9, f'slope should be 1.4, got {w}. Check that the numerator pairs x_i with its own y_i (zip), not every x with every y'
assert abs(b - 0.5) < 1e-9, f'intercept should be 0.5 = y_bar - w * x_bar, got {b}'

tests.name: residuals sum to zero
tests.code:
xs=[1.2,2.0,2.9,3.8,4.6]; ys=[2.6,2.1,4.2,3.3,5.0]
w, b = fit_line(xs, ys)
r = [y - (w*x + b) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)]
assert abs(sum(r)) < 1e-9, f'with an intercept the residuals must add to 0 (they are perpendicular to the ones column); they add to {sum(r):.4f}'
assert w != 0, 'w is still 0: compute it from num / den'

tests.name: vertical data is rejected

hints: num = sum((x - x_bar) * (y - y_bar) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)). A nested loop would pair every x with every y, which is a different (wrong) sum.
den = sum((x - x_bar) ** 2 for x in xs). Then: if den == 0: raise ValueError("all x values are equal")
w = num / den and b = y_bar - w * x_bar.
problems.solution:
def fit_line(xs, ys):
    n = len(xs)
    x_bar = sum(xs) / n
    y_bar = sum(ys) / n
    num = sum((x - x_bar) * (y - y_bar) for x, y in zip(xs, ys))
    den = sum((x - x_bar) ** 2 for x in xs)
    if den == 0:
        raise ValueError("all x values are equal")
    w = num / den
    b = y_bar - w * x_bar
    return w, b

problems.title: Normal equations in NumPy
problems.prompt:
Now with matrices. X has one row per example and one column per feature, already including a column of ones. Write fit_normal(X, y) that returns the weight vector w solving the normal equations

Xᵀ X w = Xᵀ y

tests.name: recovers slope and intercept
tests.code:
w = fit_normal(X_demo, price)
assert w is not None, 'fit_normal returned None'
assert np.shape(w) == (2,), f'expected one weight per column, shape (2,), got {np.shape(w)}'
assert abs(w[0] - 3) < 0.2 and abs(w[1] - 2) < 0.6, f'expected roughly [3, 2] for this data, got {w}'

tests.name: matches lstsq
tests.code:
r2 = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.column_stack([r2.normal(size=30), r2.normal(size=30), np.ones(30)])
y = r2.normal(size=30)
w = fit_normal(X, y)
ref = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
assert np.allclose(w, ref), f'should match np.linalg.lstsq: {ref}, got {w}. Did you use X.T @ X (shape (3, 3)) and X.T @ y?'

tests.name: residual is perpendicular to every column
tests.code:
yh = project(X_demo, price)
assert yh is not None and np.shape(yh) == (50,), f'project should return one prediction per example, shape (50,), got {np.shape(yh)}'
r = price - yh
assert np.allclose(X_demo.T @ r, 0, atol=1e-8), f'X.T @ (y - y_hat) should be ~0, got {X_demo.T @ r}'

tests.name: projecting twice changes nothing
tests.code:
yh = project(X_demo, price)
assert np.allclose(project(X_demo, yh), yh), 'a vector already on the plane is its own shadow: project(X, project(X, y)) should equal project(X, y)'
